Probably nothing is wrong. Getting out of breath after two minutes is common when you're new to running, because your lungs, heart and leg muscles haven't adapted yet, and it usually improves within a few weeks. I can't rule anything out without knowing your health history, so the exceptions are below.

Run slower than feels right. You should be able to talk in full sentences, and if you can't, slow down or walk. Most beginners go too fast, which is why two minutes feels impossible.

Try 1 minute running and 1 minute walking, repeated 8 to 10 times, after 5 minutes of brisk walking to warm up. Do it 3 times a week with a rest day between, since your body adapts during recovery. As the weeks go on, make the running parts longer and the walking parts shorter. Measure progress by how long you can run before you need to walk, not by speed.

See a doctor before you push harder if you get chest pain or pressure, dizziness, fainting, or unusual wheezing or coughing when you exercise, or if you have a heart condition or asthma you haven't talked about with a doctor. Breathlessness alone usually just means you're getting fitter, but those symptoms are worth getting checked.

Five working, three dead. At two in the morning the hum of the five sounds like an apology.

Dev comes in at ten past, a bag of whites under one arm, phone in the other hand. He nods. She nods back.

"Seven's knackered as well," she says. "And two. And four."

"That's three." He counts them on the hand with the phone in it. "Since when?"

"Since Sunday. The man's coming."

"Which man?"

She doesn't say. He sets the bag on the folding table and sorts: socks, shirts, a Partick Thistle top he handles like it might wake up. Tuesdays and Thursdays, four years. She has never once seen him use the dryers without asking which is warmest.

Under the float tin behind the counter, the envelope from the solicitor. Friday, eleven o'clock. The buyer is keeping the name. The buyer wants the machines too, or what's left of them.

"Six is warm," she says.

"Cheers, Fi." He feeds in coins. "I've an interview Monday and this is the only shirt that fits."

"Monday."

"Eight-thirty. Don't tell my mum I'm sorting it at two in the morning."

"I'll not."

She counts the float again, though she knows the number. Out on Duke Street a bus goes by, lit up and empty. Card reader, the buyer's letter said, in the second paragraph. Coins phased out by spring.

"You all right?" Dev says.

"Aye. Tired."

The drum turns. He pulls out a chair, then stops with his hand on it.

"Same time Thursday, then?"

Fiona opens the tin, looks at the notes, and shuts it.

"Mind the door on your way," she says. "It sticks."
